title: Path-Reporting Distance Oracles for Vertex-Labeled Graphs
classifications: Theory of computation → Sparsification and spanners
abstract:
Let G = (V,E) be a weighted undirected graph, with n vertices. A distance oracle is a data structure that can quickly answer distance queries, with some stretch factor. A seminal work of [Thorup and Zwick, 2005], given an integer k ≥ 1, provides such an oracle with stretch 2k-1, query time O(k), and size O(k⋅ n^{1+1/k}). Furthermore, this oracle can also report a path in G corresponding to the returned distance.
In this paper we focus on vertex-labeled graphs, in which each vertex is given a label from a set L of size 𝓁. A vertex-label distance oracle answers queries of the form (v,λ), where v ∈ V and λ ∈ L, by reporting (an approximation to) the distance from v to the closest vertex of label λ. Following [Danny Hermelin et al., 2011], it was shown in [Chechik, 2012] that for any integer k > 1, there exists a vertex-label distance oracle with stretch 4k-5, query time O(k), and size O(k⋅ n⋅ 𝓁^{1/k}). 
This state-of-the-art result suffers from two main drawbacks: The stretch is roughly a factor of 2 larger than in [Thorup and Zwick, 2005], and it is not path-reporting. We address these concerns in this work, and provide the following results.  
- First, we devise a path-reporting vertex-label distance oracle, at the cost of a slight increase in stretch and size. For any constant 0 < ε < 1, our oracle has stretch (4k-5)⋅(1+ε), query time O(k), and size O(n^{1+o(1)}⋅ 𝓁^{1/k}). 
- Second, we show how to improve the stretch to the optimal 2k-1, at the cost of mildly increasing the query time. Specifically, we devise a vertex-label distance oracle with stretch 2k-1, query time O(𝓁^{1/k}⋅log n), and size O(k⋅ n⋅ 𝓁^{1/k}).

       Abstract
Let G = (V, E) be a weighted undirected graph, with n vertices. A distance oracle is a data structure
that can quickly answer distance queries, with some stretch factor. A seminal work of [16], given an
integer k ≥ 1, provides such an oracle with stretch 2k − 1, query time O(k), and size O(k · n1+1/k ).
Furthermore, this oracle can also report a path in G corresponding to the returned distance.
    In this paper we focus on vertex-labeled graphs, in which each vertex is given a label from a
set L of size ℓ. A vertex-label distance oracle answers queries of the form (v, λ), where v ∈ V and
λ ∈ L, by reporting (an approximation to) the distance from v to the closest vertex of label λ.
Following [9], it was shown in [2] that for any integer k > 1, there exists a vertex-label distance
oracle with stretch 4k − 5, query time O(k), and size O(k · n · ℓ1/k ).
    This state-of-the-art result suffers from two main drawbacks: The stretch is roughly a factor
of 2 larger than in [16], and it is not path-reporting. We address these concerns in this work, and
provide the following results.
    First, we devise a path-reporting vertex-label distance oracle, at the cost of a slight increase in
    stretch and size. For any constant 0 < ϵ < 1, our oracle has stretch (4k − 5) · (1 + ϵ), query time
    O(k), and size O(n1+o(1) · ℓ1/k ).
    Second, we show how to improve the stretch to the optimal 2k − 1, at the cost of mildly increasing
    the query time. Specifically, we devise a vertex-label distance oracle with stretch 2k − 1, query
    time O(ℓ1/k · log n), and size O(k · n · ℓ1/k ).

       the size and query time were improved to O(n1+1/k ) and O(1) respectively, [17, 3]. This

           A useful feature of a distance oracle is its ability to report not just an approximation
        ˜ v) to the distance, but also provide a path in G between u, v of length d(u,
       d(u,                                                                               ˜ v). An
       oracle with this property is called path-reporting. The original construction of [16] provides
       a path-reporting oracle, albeit the improved one of [3] does not. Recently there has been
       a surge of interest in path-reporting distance oracles [5, 6, 1, 14, 7, 4], most of these were
       interested in obtaining (almost) linear size, as the [16] oracles always have size Ω(n log n).
           When stating the query time of path-reporting oracles, we will follow the convention of
       omitting the length of the returned path. That is, if the algorithm returns a path P in time
       O(q + |P |), we will write that the query time is O(q) (since reporting P will always incur
       time O(|P |)).


       1.1    Vertex-Label Distance Oracles
       In this paper we focus on distance oracles for vertex-labeled graphs, introduced by [9]. In
       this setting, there is a set L = {λ1 , . . . , λℓ } of labels, and each vertex receives a single label
       from L. We would like to answer vertex-label queries, which are queries of the form (v, λ),
       for v ∈ V and λ ∈ L, and the goal is to return an approximation for dist(v, λ), which is the
       distance from v to the nearest vertex of label λ.
           Vertex-label queries arise naturally in various applications, where there are multiple
       vertices that can provide a service to the source vertex v. For instance, in a network, the
       labels may indicate different types of servers that provide certain functionality, or in a road
       network, the labels may correspond to services such as gas, food, accommodation, etc. We
       would like to be able to answer queries such as “how close is the nearest gas station”, rather
       than the distance to a particular one.
           In [9] it was shown that the distance oracles of [16] can be adapted to the vertex-label
       query setting, with stretch 4k − 5 and size O(kn1+1/k ), regardless of the number of labels, ℓ.
       However, if ℓ < n1/k , then this size is larger than the trivial solution with stretch 1 and
       size O(n · ℓ), that simply stores all distances between vertices and labels. To address this
       issue, Hermelin et al. [9] devised an oracle with improved size of O(kn · ℓ1/k ), at the cost
       of increasing the stretch to 2k − 1. In [2], the stretch was substantially improved to 4k − 5.
       Both results have query time O(k).
           The current state-of-the-art leaves two main concerns. The first is that unlike standard
       distance oracles, the vertex-label oracles of [9, 2] of size ≈ n · ℓ1/k are not path-reporting.
       Indeed, for many applications the ability to report paths seems appealing (for instance,
       rather than obtaining just the distance to the nearest gas station, we would like to receive a
       path to it). The second concern is that the stretch is roughly a factor of 2 away from the
       conjectured optimum.


       1.2    Our Results
       In this paper we provide a positive answer to both concerns mentioned above. That is, by
       slightly increasing the stretch, we show how to obtain path-reporting vertex-label distance
       oracles. In addition, we show a construction that achieves the optimal stretch of 2k − 1, at
       the cost of mildly increasing the query time.

has stretch (4k − 5) · (1 + ϵ) and size O(n1+o(1) · ℓ1/k ). (Alternatively, with stretch O(k) and

    Our second result achieves for any integer k > 1, a vertex-label distance oracle with
stretch 2k − 1, size O(k · n · ℓ1/k ), and query time O(ℓ1/k · log n). (This oracle can also be
made path-reporting, at the cost of increasing the stretch by a factor of 1 + ϵ, and the size
by a factor of no(1) .)


1.3      Overview of Techniques
Our construction of the path-reporting vertex-label distance oracle starts similarly to previous
works [9, 2]. Given the integer parameter k > 1, we sample a sequence of sets V = A0 ⊇
A1 ⊇ ... ⊇ Ak−1 ⊇ Ak = ∅, as follows. For each 0 ≤ i ≤ k − 2, every vertex in Ai is
independently sampled to Ai+1 with probability ℓ−1/k (recall that ℓ = |L| is the number of
labels). This sampling probability is different from the n−1/k used in [16], which allows the
size improvement from ≈ n1+1/k to ≈ n · ℓ1/k . However, the main issue is that the last set
                                                  n
Ak−1 is expected to be prohibitively large, ℓ1−1/k   .
    As in [16], for each v ∈ V and 0 ≤ i ≤ k − 1 define pivots: pi (v) is the nearest vertex
of Ai to v, and bunches: Bi (v) contains all the vertices in Ai closer to v than pi+1 (v), and
         S
B(v) = i Bi (v). The cluster of u ∈ V , C(u), consists of all vertices v such that u ∈ B(v).
    Path-reporting construction: The query algorithm of [2], given the query (v, λ), finds a
pivot pi (v) such that there exists some vertex u of label λ with pi (v) ∈ B(u). It then returns
the sum of distances from u, v to this pivot pi (v). We take a similar approach, and as long as
i < k − 1, we can apply the technique of [16], using clusters, to find a path from v to u via the
cluster of pi (v). The issue arises when i = k − 1, then the clusters of vertices in this last level
Ak−1 are too large to store. To overcome this hurdle, we apply a pairwise path-reporting
distance oracle, that approximately preserves distances (and reports paths), only between a
given set of pairs. Indeed, we show that the set of pairs containing all the possible required
connections for vertices in Ak−1 is sufficiently small, and the pairwise oracles of [7, 14] induce
a slight increase in stretch and size.
    Improved stretch: The query algorithm mentioned above, given a query (v, λ), tests only
the pivots of v. This one-sided testing enables stretch of 4k − 5, similarly to the context of
compact routing schemes [15], where we have access to the bunches of the source v, but not
to the bunches of the destination u. In order to obtain the (conjectured) optimal stretch of
2k − 1 for vertex-label queries, we need two-sided testing, as in [16, 3], where we also inspect
whether the pivots of the destination u are in B(v). Alas, the destination u is not known,
we are only given a label λ. In order to achieve two-sided testing, it seems that in the i-th
iteration, one must check for each vertex u of label λ, whether pi (u) ∈ B(v). Unfortunately,
this may result in a linear query time. To deal with this barrier, in the pre-processing phase,
for each λ ∈ L, we store all the level i pivots of vertices with label λ, denoted Pi (λ), in a
hash table. Then, we can check if there exists a vertex of Bi (v) in Pi (λ). This will be much
faster, since the size of Bi (v), for i < k − 1, is bounded by ≈ ℓ1/k . As the last set of level
k − 1 can be quite large, we will need to treat it differently, which leads to an intricate case
analysis when bounding the stretch.

       1.4        Related Work
       In the context of planar graphs, [13] showed a vertex-label distance oracle with stretch
       1 + ϵ, size O(n log n) and query time O(log n · log ∆), where 0 < ϵ < 1 is fixed and ∆ is
       the hop-diameter of the graph. This result is somewhat inferior to state-of-the-art distance
       oracles for planar graph, where [12] obtained stretch 1 + ϵ, size O(n) and query time O(1).
       In [8], a stretch 1 vertex-label distance oracle for planar graphs is shown, with parameters
       (size and query) that are at most polylogarithmically larger than the standard setting.
           A closely related problem is the so-called colored distance oracles, which can answer
       label-to-label queries. These objects were studied by [11, 10], in the context of detecting
       patterns in texts, focusing on the 1 + ϵ stretch regime.


           2      Preliminaries

       Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph with nonnegative weights on the edges w : E → R+ .
       Given a set L of labels, each vertex is associated with a single label λ ∈ L. For λ ∈ L, the
       set of vertices of label λ is denoted by Vλ .
           For vertices u, v ∈ V , define dist(u, v) as the length of the shortest path between u, v
       with respect to the weights. If H is a subgraph of G, we denote distH (u, v) the distance in H.
       For a vertex v ∈ V and a set A ⊆ V , define dist(v, A) = minu∈A {dist(v, u)}. Additionally,
       let dist(v, ∅) = ∞.
           For every vertex v ∈ V and label λ ∈ L, we define λ(v) as the closest node to v that has
       the label λ, that is, dist(v, λ(v)) = dist(v, Vλ ).

           Pairwise distance oracles: Given a set of pairs P ⊆ V × V , a pairwise distance oracle is
       required to (approximately) answer distance queries only for pairs in P. A pairwise oracle
       is called path-reporting if it can also return a path in G that achieves the approximated
       distance. We will use two results: the first from [7] that has stretch close to 1, and the
